docs.title: ADR: 以 CephFS 取代 JuiceFS 作為跨 namespace / 跨 pod 的多租戶家目錄
docs.text:
• 狀態：CONDITIONAL GO — 技術已在實機驗證，受限於硬體容量
  • 日期：2026-08-15
  • 決策者：平台工程
  • 原始數據：inventory/benchmark/2026-08-15/
  • 相關：.kiro/specs/production-rook-ceph-cilium-multus（Requirement 8、9），inventory/ownership-ledger/2026-08-15-storage-ownership.md

docs.title: 1. 脈絡
docs.text:
多租戶的個人 storage 必須同時掛進不同 namespace（使用者的 personal namespace、其參與的 project namespace）與不同 pod（IDE、訓練任務、fast-stage job）。在 Kubernetes 中這就是 RWX 需求。

平台過去的兩條路都不理想：

方案 機制 問題 Longhorn RWX 每個 volume 一個 NFS-Ganesha share-manager pod（pkg/k8s/volume_share_nfs.go） 單點、效能差，2026-08 已退役，文件記載為「the dominant source of storage is slow reports」 JuiceFS（現況） FUSE + TiKV metadata，static PV 複製 CSI 區塊（pkg/k8s/volume_share_juicefs.go） 每次 namespace 變更都要一次 TiKV Raft 共識，建檔 2 918 µs 且快取無效

問題：CephFS 能不能取代 JuiceFS，同時不再掉回 NFS？

docs.title: 2. 決策
docs.text:
可以。採用 CephFS 作為跨 namespace 家目錄 lane，維持 canonical PVC + static mirror 的模式，隔離沿用現況等級（單一平台 CephX key）。

三個理由，全部已在本叢集實測驗證：

docs.title: 2.1 CephFS 原生 RWX，資料路徑完全沒有 NFS
docs.text:
多個 pod／node／namespace 直接掛同一個檔案系統，一致性由 MDS 的 capability lease 維持。實測結果：

PASS  same home directory visible from all namespaces and nodes
PASS  no NFS volume source and no share-manager pod (native RWX)
PASS  cross-node visibility in 208 ms (write ns-A -> read ns-C)
PASS  concurrent writes from 3 namespaces all landed
PASS  kernel CephFS mount (no FUSE)

驗證腳本：scripts/storage/cephfs-shared-home-validate.sh（3 個 namespace × 3 個節點）。 208 ms 含 kubectl exec 往返開銷，實際檔案系統可見性遠低於此；對照 JuiceFS 需等 30 秒 entry-cache TTL。

docs.title: 2.2 效能：對 JuiceFS 有數量級改善
docs.text:
同一套 harness、同一組參數、3 次取中位數：

Metadata 操作 local-scratch JuiceFS CephFS CephFS vs JuiceFS create p50 18.6 µs 2 918 µs 278 µs 快 10.5× unlink p50 13.1 µs 2 882 µs 275 µs 快 10.5× stat p50（cold） 2.80 µs 7.44 µs 5.03 µs 快 1.5× stat p99（cold） 3.38 µs 755 µs 11.6 µs 尾延遲好 65×

使用者實際感受得到的工作負載（20 000 個小檔）：

工作負載 local-scratch JuiceFS CephFS CephFS vs JuiceFS git init + git add -A 0.32 s 84.19 s 0.56 s 快 150× git status（cold） 0.06 s 1.69 s 0.09 s 快 19× git status（warm） 0.07 s 0.67 s 0.07 s 快 9.6×（與本機同速） 解壓 20 000 個小檔 0.73 s 237.34 s 8.44 s 快 28× 刪除全部檔案 0.48 s 58.28 s 9.32 s 快 6.3× 掃描 + stat 全部 0.17 s 1.58 s 0.59 s 快 2.7×

最關鍵的一點：git status 與 git init/add 在 CephFS 上幾乎等同本機速度（0.07 s vs 0.07 s；0.56 s vs 0.32 s），而在 JuiceFS 上分別慢 10× 與 267×。這正是使用者日常抱怨的操作。

但誠實說明：CephFS 沒有消除與本機的差距，只是把它縮小。批次建檔／刪檔仍慢 11–19×（解壓 8.44 s vs 0.73 s）。任何分散式檔案系統都不會等於本機；延遲敏感的暫存工作仍應使用 local-scratch。

docs.title: 2.3 歸因得到驗證
docs.text:
先前的 cold/warm 拆解指出 JuiceFS 的瓶頸是遠端 metadata round-trip（stat cold p99 755 µs vs warm 8.2 µs），而 create 冷熱皆 ~2.9 ms 表示快取原理上救不了寫入——每次 namespace 變更都是一次 TiKV Raft 共識。

CephFS 用單跳到 MDS 的記憶體 cache 取代它，實測 278 µs 正好落在事前預測的 200–500 µs 區間。假說成立。

docs.title: 3. 架構
docs.text:
沿用平台既有的 canonical / mirror 模式（spec Requirement 8），與 JuiceFS 的作法同構：

canonical dynamic PVC (rook-cephfs-pilot SC)
  └─ subvolumePath = /volumes/csi/csi-vol-<uuid>/<uuid>
       ├─ mirror PV (ns A) : staticVolume=true, rootPath=<同上>, volumeHandle=唯一
       ├─ mirror PV (ns B) : 同 rootPath，volumeHandle 不同
       └─ ...

實作於 pkg/k8s/volume_share_cephfs.go。pkg/k8s/volume_share.go 的 driver switch 加一個 case 即可，五個呼叫端（IDE、executor、configfile、storage control plane、fast transfer）一行都不用改。

與 JuiceFS 路徑的三個關鍵差異：

JuiceFS CephFS volumeHandle 直接沿用來源 每個 mirror 必須唯一 —— ceph-csi 以此為內部狀態索引，重複會衝突 volumeAttributes 原樣複製 加 staticVolume: "true"、rootPath；移除 subvolumeName 等 provisioner 記帳欄位，否則 ceph-csi 會誤認 mirror 由它建立而可刪除 reclaim policy Retain Retain（強制） —— ceph-csi 官方明示不支援 static PV 的 subvolume 刪除

mirror 的相等性以 rootPath 比對，不是 volumeHandle——因為 handle 刻意不同。

docs.title: 4. 隔離模型
docs.text:
現階段：單一平台 CephX key，只存在於 rook-ceph namespace，租戶取不到。 隔離由 K8s RBAC 保證（租戶不能自建 static PV）。這與現行 JuiceFS 把 secret 放在 juicefs-system 的模式完全相同，不是安全退步。

必須記錄的限制：CephFS 的 path-restricted CephX（ceph fs authorize <fs> client.X /path rw）只限制 MDS 的目錄階層。官方明言：

"This restriction impacts only the filesystem hierarchy... Clients will still be able to access the underlying file data in RADOS directly."

因為 osd cap 是 allow rw tag cephfs data=<fs>，涵蓋整個 data pool。因此 path 限制不可單獨作為對抗惡意租戶的安全邊界。

升級路徑（JuiceFS 沒有的能力）：以 --namespace-isolated 建立 subvolume，讓每個租戶的資料位於獨立 RADOS namespace，再配合 per-PV nodeStageSecretRef 發放 path-restricted key。本階段先不啟用，但 subvolume 一開始就用該選項建立，日後收緊不需搬資料。

docs.title: 5. 現況部署（Pilot）
docs.text:
項目 值 Rook v1.20.4（支援 K8s v1.31–v1.36，本叢集 v1.35.0） Ceph v20.2.3 Tentacle（v20.2.0 因資料毀損告警為 NO-GO） Ceph-CSI v3.17.0，kernel client（cephFsClientType: kernel） 拓樸 MON×3、MGR×2、OSD×3（每 node 一個）、MDS 1 active + 1 hot standby（跨節點） Pool metadata + data 皆 replica 3、failureDomain=host 容量 1.8 TiB raw → 570 GiB 可用（每 OSD 600 GiB） StorageClass cephfs（production lane）與 rook-cephfs-pilot（benchmark 基準，勿動），皆 non-default；longhorn 仍為 cluster default 平台預設 lane DEFAULT_STORAGE_CLASS_NAME: cephfs —— 同時作用於 personal home 與 group storage 網路 Cilium pod 網路，未新增 Multus NAD（B-004 未解除）

MDS failover 已實測：刪除 active MDS 後 standby 立即接手，全程 1/1 daemons up。

docs.title: 6. 這個 Pilot 不能證明什麼
docs.text:
OSD 是 /data 上的 loop-backed 檔案，因為三台九顆 NVMe 已 100% 配置給已掛載的 XFS，且 XFS 不可 shrink（見 ownership ledger）。堆疊為：

/data/ceph-pilot/osd0.img (fallocate 200 GiB, 非 sparse)
  → losetup --direct-io=on → pvcreate → vg_ceph_pilot → lvcreate → Rook

疊 LVM 是因為 Rook 官方列出「LVM Logical Volumes」為支援的 OSD 型態，loop device 則完全未出現在文件中。

因此：

  • 這不是 production 組態，不可用於容量規劃或 SLO。
  • 正面結果具結論性：CephFS 在多一層 XFS 的handicap下仍勝 JuiceFS 10×，真實硬體只會更好。
  • 資料路徑數字（fio）偏保守，metadata 數字則可信度高，因為瓶頸在 MDS 而非 OSD 吞吐。

docs.title: 7. 已知問題與風險
docs.text: 項目 說明 處置 GPU2 容量 分配 200 GiB 後 /data 達 75%，Ceph 正確發出 MON_DISK_LOW（mon a 僅 25% 可用，門檻 30%） 保留此告警不靜音 —— 它是 GPU2 為容量瓶頸的真實訊號 mgr 模組崩潰 已根治 prometheus mgr 模組每 15 秒向 orchestrator 要 node-proxy 硬體資料，而 Rook 的 orchestrator 未實作 node_proxy_fullreport，每次輪詢都拋 NotImplementedError 並記一次 crash —— 數小時累積 248 次，把叢集永久釘在 HEALTH_WARN，遮蔽真正的警告 停用 prometheus mgr 模組（cephClusterSpec.mgr.modules）。此處無人消費它：monitoring.enabled: false、無 rook-ceph 的 ServiceMonitor、Prometheus 的 active ceph target 為 0。停用後 150 秒內新 crash 為 0，叢集回到真正的 HEALTH_OK。日後若要 Ceph metrics，需連同 monitoring 一起開，並預期 crash 噪音回歸直到 Rook 實作該呼叫 BlueStore probe IO error ×2 KernelDevice.cc "Unexpected IO error"，來自 OSD prepare 期間的 ceph-bluestore-tool 探測 非來自運行中的 OSD；三個 OSD 0 次重啟、26 分鐘 active+clean、已寫入 175 MiB／100k dentries。屬 loop 非受支援型態的表徵，production 應改用真實 block device VolumeSnapshot 未驗證 叢集完全沒有 external-snapshotter CRD（只有 snapshots.longhorn.io） 安裝需 cluster-wide 變更並會同時影響 Longhorn，刻意不做，另案決定 static PV 限制 mirror 不支援 snapshot/clone/expand；backing subvolume 需人工清理 生命週期操作一律只對 canonical ceph-csi #2238 static volume 的 global mount/unmount leak 列入監控與 node runbook B-004 網路 25G/10G 同在 192.168.110.0/24 Pilot 走 pod 網路規避；production 前必須解決

docs.title: 8. 部署過程中發現的陷阱（會讓人以為成功其實沒有）
docs.text:
1. Rook 1.20 chart 已無 enableCephfsDriver / forceCephFSKernelClient 等 key。 Helm 靜默接受未知 values，設了等於沒設。CSI 改由 ceph-csi-operator 的 Driver CR 控制（deploy/rook-pilot/cephfs-driver.yaml）。
  2. chart 不會建立 CSI plugin 的 ServiceAccount。 缺少時 Driver CR 會回報 reconcile 成功，但 ReplicaSet/DaemonSet 靜默失敗於 error looking up service account，PVC 永遠 Pending。需套用 deploy/rook-pilot/cephfs-csi-rbac.yaml，且 csiServiceAccountPrefix 必須與其名稱一致。
  3. loop device 預設 DIO 0（buffered）。 BlueStore 的 O_DIRECT/fsync 會被主機 page cache 吸收 —— Ceph 誤以為資料已落盤（durability 風險），且寫入延遲被 RAM 灌水。必須 losetup --direct-io=on，並寫進開機 helper。
  4. MDS active 與 standby 預設可能排在同一 node（首次安裝時兩者都在 gpu1），使 standby 形同虛設。需 podAntiAffinity。

docs.title: 已完成的平台接線（2026-08-15）
docs.text:
1. 容量擴充至 570 GiB 可用（每 OSD 200 → 600 GiB）。空間全部來自 GPU2 的 containerd 垃圾回收：810 G → 427 G，/data 由 75% 降到 54%，回收約 383 GB。成因是 201 個 image 中有 103 個未被引用，且 534 個 Active snapshot 只對應 167 個運行中容器 —— 已退出容器的 snapshot 未被清理。因此不需要動任何 Longhorn 資料就達成了 3× 擴充。
  2. CephFS 成為 personal home 與 group storage 的新建預設：DEFAULT_STORAGE_CLASS_NAME: cephfs。該值同時驅動 user_storage_manager.go（個人家目錄）與 policy_options.go（group storage 預設選項），一個值即切換兩者。既有 PVC 完全不動；JuiceFS 降為 restricted: true 的相容 lane。
  3. backend：SemanticStorageLane() 與 inferStorageBackend/RecommendedFor/Description 加入 cephfs 分支。
  4. frontend：StorageProfileBadge 的 backendFor()/badgeStyle() 加入 cephfs，補上 storage.backend_cephfs（en/zh），並把 group storage 文案改為 backend-neutral —— 原本硬寫「共享 longhorn pool / Longhorn 儲存策略」，在預設改變後會誤導。

docs.title: 後續
docs.text:
1. 未遷移任何既有 production 資料 —— 只有新建的 storage 走 CephFS。
  2. GPU2 容量瓶頸 已再處理一輪（2026-08-15）：
  3. Prometheus 的 121 G 其實是 snapshot 膨脹：60 GiB 的 volume 掛著 7 個 8–9 天前的 snapshot（72.6 GiB）。根因是 platform-daily-snapshot-delete CronJob 被 suspend（SUSPEND: True，8 天沒跑），保留策略從未生效；建立用的 platform-hourly-snapshot job 已被移除但舊 snapshot 留著。清掉後 Prometheus 由 121 G 降到 60 G。
  4. 三個 monitoring volume 已搬離 gpu2 /data，並由 1 副本提升為 2 副本跨 2 節點，順帶消除單點風險。
  5. 清除 9 個孤兒 Released Longhorn PV（JuiceFS TiKV/PD 遷移到 local-metadata 後的殘留，38.6 GiB 實際 / 1080 Gi provisioned）。Longhorn volume 由 36 降為 27。
  6. 結果：gpu2 /data/longhorn 133 G → 3.4 G，gpu2 /data 76% → 69%。
  7. 磁碟使用政策已套用：Longhorn 在 gpu1/gpu2/gpu3 一律使用 /data；/data2 於 gpu2、gpu3 皆設 allowScheduling: false，因為該磁碟存放他人以 hostPath 存取的個人資料。
  8. /data2 決定不搬遷（他人以 hostPath 存取的個人資料）。已停止新排程，既有 replica 與資料一律不動。約 1.5 TB 平台 Longhorn 資料仍在其上（harbor-gpu23-registry 433 G、platform-build-scratch 236 G、harbor-registry 187 G 為最大三筆）。

快照回收的修正：我原先以「加總各 snapshot 的 size 欄位」估出 /data2 有 838 GiB 可回收，這個估法是錯的。Longhorn 的 snapshot size 是該快照磁碟檔的大小，而在快照鏈中最舊的那個持有幾乎全部的 volume 資料、較新的只有增量 —— 加總會把「live 資料」重複計算。實際回收只有約 17–32 GB。Prometheus 那筆（121 → 60 GiB）是真的，因為它有 7 個彼此重疊、確實過期的快照。評估 Longhorn 快照可回收量應以 volume 的 actualSize 前後差值為準，不可加總 snapshot size。 5. Longhorn numberOfReplicas: 1 仍是獨立風險：其餘 volume 多數仍為單副本。與 CephFS 無關，建議另案處理。 4. 仍為 loop-backed OSD，不可用於 SLO 或容量規劃；取得真實 block device 後需重測。 5. 決定是否安裝 external-snapshotter 以驗證 snapshot/restore。

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: Welcome to the GPU Cluster Management Platform. This guide covers everything you need to use the platform — from signing in to launching GPU-powered workspaces.

docs.title: What You Can Do
docs.text:
The platform lets you:

  • Launch GPU workspaces (JupyterLab, VSCode, custom images) backed by persistent storage
  • Manage projects with defined GPU/CPU/memory quotas, versioned config files, and team members
  • Collaborate in groups with shared storage and role-based access
  • Submit requests for additional resources, storage, or image access
  • Read announcements for maintenance windows, incidents, and policy updates
  • Monitor your resource usage and active GPU jobs from the dashboard

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• A modern web browser (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari)
  • An account provisioned by a platform administrator
  • (Optional) VPN access if the platform is deployed on a private network

docs.title: Platform Navigation
docs.text:
graph TD
    Login[Sign In] --> Home[Home Dashboard]

    subgraph Workspace
        Home --> Projects[Projects]
        Home --> Workspaces[Workspaces / IDEs]
    end

    subgraph Resources
        Home --> Groups[Groups]
        Home --> Storage[Storage]
    end

    subgraph Infrastructure
        Home --> Announcements[Announcements]
        Home --> Requests[Requests]
        Home --> Settings[Settings]
    end

The left sidebar organises features into four sections:

Section Features Home Dashboard overview Workspace Projects, Workspaces (IDEs) Resources Groups, Storage Infrastructure Announcements, Requests, Settings

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
See the Getting Started guide for the complete step-by-step walkthrough — from VPN setup to launching your first GPU workspace.

First-time checklist

  • [ ] Connect to VPN
  • [ ] Sign in at https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  • [ ] Explore the Home Dashboard
  • [ ] Check your project's GPU quota under Projects
  • [ ] Launch your first workspace

docs.title: Role Summary
docs.text:
Role Description User Regular platform user; can use resources within allocated quotas Manager Can manage projects and groups; elevated admin-panel access Admin Full platform control; access to all admin functions

See Concepts & Roles for detailed permission tables.

docs.title: Announcements
docs.text:
Announcements are platform-wide messages from administrators. They appear as dashboard banners and stay on the Announcements page until they expire. Scheduled announcements stay hidden until their publish time.

Access: All authenticated users.

docs.title: Where Announcements Appear
docs.text:
Location What You See Home Dashboard Pinned or unread announcements appear near the top of the page. Sidebar → Announcements Full list of active announcements with All and Unread filters. Modal view Full title, content, priority, publish date, and expiry date.

Announcements can have info, warning, or critical priority. Critical notices usually describe maintenance, service degradation, or actions users must take.

docs.title: Read and Acknowledge
docs.text:
1. Open Announcements from the sidebar, or click View all on a dashboard banner.
  2. Select an announcement to open the detail modal.
  3. Opening an unread announcement marks it as read for your account.

Pinned announcements may continue to appear even after you read them, until an administrator unpins or expires them.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
Why did an announcement disappear?

The announcement probably reached its expiry time or was removed by an administrator.

Can I reply to an announcement?

No. Use Requests if you need help or want to ask about a notice.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
Use cscc-cli to authenticate, submit image builds, stream build logs, and manage your own API tokens.

Access: All authenticated users.

docs.title: Login
docs.text:
On a new machine, give the CLI the API URL explicitly with --api-url or CSCC_API_URL. The value may include /api/v1; the CLI normalizes it for you.

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

The CLI prompts for your password. Unlike the dashboard, this flow needs no CAPTCHA.

On success, the CLI saves a cscc_... API token in its local config file, readable only by you. The token value itself is shown only once when it is created.

Optional token name:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice --name workstation

Token names are limited to 100 characters. Leave the flag off to use the default name, cscc-cli.

docs.title: Import a dashboard-created token
docs.text:
You can also create an API token from Settings → API Key & CLI in the dashboard and import it into cscc-cli:

cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --token cscc_...

The CLI verifies the token before saving it. This is handy when you are already signed in to the dashboard and would rather not type your password in a terminal.

docs.title: Stateless token override
docs.text:
For automation, set CSCC_API_TOKEN instead of saving local config:

CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw CSCC_API_TOKEN=cscc_... cscc-cli whoami

CSCC_DEV_TOKEN is still accepted as a deprecated compatibility alias, but new scripts should use CSCC_API_TOKEN.

docs.title: TLS / Internal CA
docs.text:
Official cscc-cli releases already trust the platform's certificate, so most users never need to configure one. If the platform certificate is rotated, download the latest CLI release before reconnecting.

The variables below are only for custom builds and TLS troubleshooting:

Env Description CSCC_API_URL API base URL, e.g. https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw/api/v1 CSCC_API_TOKEN Optional stateless cscc_... token override CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH One or multiple PEM files separated by , or ; CSCC_API_TLS_SERVER_NAME Optional TLS SNI name (fallback to config if not set) SSL_CERT_FILE Path to a PEM file containing the internal root CA REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE Alternative env path for a PEM bundle containing the internal root CA

Example:

CSCC_API_CA_CERT_PATH=/Users/me/platform-internal-root-ca.pem \
  cscc-cli login --api-url https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw --username alice

docs.title: Check Identity
docs.text:
cscc-cli whoami

This verifies the saved token and prints your current user and role. Role changes take effect immediately.

docs.title: Build Images
docs.text:
Upload mode is the default and accepts a directory, a .tar.gz, or a .zip archive:

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1.0.1 .
cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer ./context.tar.gz

For directories, the CLI packs the target directory into a .tar.gz build context. The context or uploaded archive must contain a root-level Dockerfile.

Dockerfile-only mode matches the dashboard's pasted-Dockerfile flow:

cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --tag v1.0.1 \
  --dockerfile ./Dockerfile

cat Dockerfile | cscc-cli build --source dockerfile \
  --project <project-id> \
  --name trainer \
  --dockerfile -

Useful options:

Option Description --project Project ID that owns the image build --name Short image name, for example trainer-api --tag Optional image tag. Omit it to use the platform default --source upload or dockerfile --dockerfile Dockerfile path, or - for stdin, when --source dockerfile --build-arg Dockerfile ARG override as KEY=VALUE; repeatable --follow=false Submit the build without streaming logs

docs.title: Build arguments
docs.text:
Pass Dockerfile ARG values at build time with --build-arg KEY=VALUE. The flag is repeatable and works with upload and dockerfile builds. Each KEY must start with a letter or underscore and contain only letters, digits, and underscores.

cscc-cli build --project <project-id> --name trainer --tag v1 \
  --build-arg HF_TOKEN=hf_xxx \
  --build-arg MAX_JOBS=4 \
  .

Use this to keep secrets and tunables out of the committed Dockerfile (for example an ARG HF_TOKEN), or to cap compile parallelism (MAX_JOBS, FLASH_ATTN_MAX_JOBS, …) so a heavy build fits the shared build engine.

Build args are visible to anyone who can inspect the build. Treat them as low-sensitivity, and rotate any token passed this way once the build is done.

docs.title: Shared build queue
docs.text:
Image builds share one build engine and run one at a time. Each build gets a fixed amount of CPU, memory, and scratch space that you cannot override.

After submission, --follow=true (the default) waits for logs to become available, streams them, and exits once the build reports completed, failed, or deleted.

The CLI takes the API endpoint from --api-url at login, then CSCC_API_URL, then its saved config:

export CSCC_API_URL=https://api.cscc.nthu.edu.tw

Builds and log streams use the token created by cscc-cli login — no other credential is needed. The project must have Image Build Permission enabled, and your project role must allow builds.

docs.title: Token Management
docs.text:
List active API tokens:

cscc-cli tokens list

Revoke a token by ID:

cscc-cli tokens revoke <token-id>

Log out from the current machine:

cscc-cli logout

Logout revokes the token in use and clears it from local config. Any manual certificate settings are kept so you can log in again without redoing them.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Setting Default Notes Token lifetime 90 days Create a new token when the old one expires Active tokens per user 20 Revoke unused tokens if you hit the limit Failed sign-ins before lockout 5 Applies to both the dashboard and the CLI Lockout duration 15 min Wait it out, or ask an admin to unlock the account

Your administrator can adjust these values for the deployment.

docs.title: Concepts & Roles
docs.text: Understanding the platform's tenancy model and permission system helps you work effectively with projects, groups, and storage.

docs.title: Tenancy Hierarchy
docs.text:
Resources on the platform are organised in a hierarchy:

graph TD
    Admin[Platform Admin] -->|creates| Group[Group\ne.g. Research Lab]
    Group -->|contains| Project[Project\ne.g. LLM Fine-Tuning]
    Project -->|launches| Workspace[Workspace / IDE]
    Project -->|binds| ProjStorage[Project Storage Volume]
    Group -->|owns| GroupStorage[Group Storage Volume]
    GroupStorage -->|inherited by| ProjStorage
Entity Description Group A team or department. Groups own shared storage and can be project members. Project The primary resource allocation unit. Holds GPU/CPU quotas, config files, and deployments. Workspace An interactive IDE (JupyterLab / VSCode) running inside the project's quota. Storage volume Persistent storage; survives workspace restarts.

docs.title: Quota Lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Admin["Admin defines\nResource Plan"] -->|assigned to| Project
    Project -->|quota enforced on| Launch[Workspace Launch]
    Launch -->|reserves| Claim["GPU claim"]
    Launch -->|uses| Queue["Scheduling queue"]
    Claim -->|allocates| GPULimit["GPU / SM share"]
    Queue -->|applies| Priority["Priority / preemption policy"]

Each project is assigned a Resource Plan by an admin. When you launch a workspace, the platform checks the project quota and your per-user quota before reserving anything.

A plan also carries:

  • An allowed GPU model list — only these models are selectable from the launch form.
  • An optional schedule window that restricts when plan-bound queues are usable (see Plan Window below).
  • One or more bound queues with their priority, preemption, and GPU-model policy.

docs.title: Scheduling Queues, Priority, and Preemption
docs.text:
Workloads choose a scheduling queue. A queue owns a priority value, an optional preemptible flag, and an optional deserved GPU limit:

Concept Meaning Priority Higher-priority queues are scheduled first when GPUs are scarce. Preemptible Workloads in this queue can be stopped to free GPUs for higher-priority queues. Deserved GPU The GPU floor a queue is guaranteed even when other queues compete. A 0 value marks a queue as a "victim" eligible to be drained first.

The default queue is always available; plan-bound queues are listed alongside it on the workspace and deploy forms.

docs.title: Plan Window
docs.text:
A plan window is the time interval during which a project's plan-bound queues are usable. Outside the window, those queues stop accepting new workloads and may stop the ones already running. Workloads on the default queue are not affected.

The dashboard shows live countdowns for the next boundary (open/close), so users can avoid eviction by switching to the default queue or waiting for the next window.

docs.title: GPU Claims
docs.text:
Every GPU on the platform is handed out through a claim. A claim describes:

  • A GPU model
  • An SM share percentage — how much of that GPU's compute you get
  • A VRAM policy — elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads, hard cap enforces a strict ceiling

There are two kinds:

  • Inline claim — created automatically when you launch a workspace. It lives and dies with that workspace.
  • Project GPU claim — created from a project's GPU Claims tab and reused across deployments. It reserves GPU quota as soon as you create it, but only accrues GPU-hours while a workload is actually attached.

Config files point at a project GPU claim through a named slot, for example platform-go/dra-claim-name: '{{ gpuClaimName "train-a" }}'. The slot name is only a label — you map it to one of your own claims in the deploy dialog. Every replica of a Deployment shares the same claim and is counted once, so split the workload into separate Deployments if only some replicas should use one.

docs.title: System Roles
docs.text: Permission User Manager Admin Use workspaces within quota ✓ ✓ ✓ Create personal projects ✓ ✓ ✓ Submit resource requests ✓ ✓ ✓ Access admin panel ✓ ✓ Manage all users / groups ✓ Define resource plans ✓ Manage platform queues ✓ View audit logs ✓ ✓ RBAC policy management ✓

docs.title: Project Roles
docs.text: Permission Member Manager Admin Launch workspaces ✓ ✓ ✓ View project configs ✓ ✓ ✓ Edit config files ✓ ✓ Manage deployments ✓ ✓ Add/remove members ✓ Delete project ✓

docs.title: Group Roles
docs.text: Permission Member Admin Access group storage ✓ ✓ View group members ✓ ✓ Add/remove members ✓ Set storage permissions ✓

docs.title: Storage Permission Model
docs.text:
Storage permissions follow a dual-path inheritance model:

flowchart TD
    GroupAdmin["Group Admin\nsets permissions"] -->|batch set| GroupStorage["Group volume\n(source of truth)"]
    GroupStorage -->|inherited, read-only| ProjectView["Project Storage View\nfor Group Members"]
    ProjectAdmin["Project Admin"] -->|direct management| DirectPerms["Project Storage\nfor Non-Group Members"]
    DirectPerms --> ProjectView
  • Group members always inherit storage permissions from the group level. Their permissions cannot be overridden at the project level.
  • Direct project members who are not in the source group have permissions managed directly at the project level. Users outside the project cannot receive project-level storage grants.

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text: Term Definition Storage volume (PVC) Persistent storage that survives workspace restarts Scheduling Queue A named policy that controls priority, preemption, queue windows, and optional GPU model affinity Plan Window The time interval during which a project's plan-bound queues are usable Preemption Stopping a workload in a preemptible queue so a higher-priority one can run GPU Claim A GPU reservation. Project claims reserve quota when created and accrue GPU-hours only while a workload is attached Config File A versioned deployment definition; every save creates a new, immutable version SM share The percentage of a GPU's compute you are allocated Resource Plan A named template defining GPU, CPU, memory limits, allowed GPU models, and schedule windows for a project Storage Lane A profile (shared-rwx, local-scratch, fast-rwo) that selects how a volume is provisioned. See Storage. Workspace An interactive cloud IDE (JupyterLab, VSCode)

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
A step-by-step guide to connecting, signing in, launching your first GPU workspace, and deploying a container.

Access: All users with a platform account provisioned by an administrator.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Details Browser Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari (latest version) Account Username and password provided by your platform admin VPN client OpenVPN-compatible client (see Step 1 below)

VPN is required

The platform runs on a private network. Connect via OpenVPN first, then use the DNS names under cscc.nthu.edu.tw; do not browse raw infrastructure URLs.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install a VPN Client
docs.text: OS Recommended Client Install Windows OpenVPN Connect Download installer from the official site macOS Tunnelblick or OpenVPN Connect brew install --cask tunnelblick Linux OpenVPN CLI sudo apt install openvpn or sudo dnf install openvpn

docs.title: Step 2 — Connect to the VPN
docs.text:
1. Obtain the Platform-VPN.ovpn configuration file — it is located at scripts/vpn/Platform-VPN.ovpn, or ask your administrator for a copy.
  2. Import it into your VPN client:
    • Windows / macOS GUI: drag the .ovpn file onto the client window, or use Import Profile.
    • Linux CLI: sudo openvpn --config scripts/vpn/Platform-VPN.ovpn
  3. When prompted, enter your platform username and password (the same credentials you use to sign in).
  4. Wait for the connection to establish — the client shows a green indicator or Initialization Sequence Completed.

Verify connectivity

Open a terminal and run: 

nslookup dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
If the name resolves and the dashboard opens, you are connected. If not, check that UDP port 31194 is not blocked by your firewall.

Windows route check

If OpenVPN shows connected but 192.168.109.1 is unreachable, open PowerShell and run route print | findstr 192.168.109. The output should include a 192.168.109.0 route through the OpenVPN adapter. If it is missing, re-import the latest Platform-VPN.ovpn.

The VPN profile accepts platform DNS for cscc.nthu.edu.tw, but does not enable block-outside-dns. Use Resolve-DnsName dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw to confirm platform DNS and http://192.168.109.1:30080 for low-level connectivity checks.

docs.title: Step 3 — Sign In to the Platform
docs.text:
1. Open your browser and navigate to: 
    https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw
  2. You will see the login page with three fields:
Field Description Username Your platform account username Password Your platform account password CAPTCHA Type the 4-character code shown in the image (case-insensitive)
  1. Fill in all three fields and click SIGN IN.

Figure 1: Login page with username, password, and CAPTCHA fields.

CAPTCHA tips

  • The code is case-insensitive — Ab3K and ab3k both work.
  • Click the CAPTCHA image to refresh it if it is hard to read.

docs.title: Step 4 — Explore the Home Dashboard
docs.text:
After login you land on the Home Dashboard at /.

Widget What It Shows GPU Availability Free vs. allocated GPU units across the cluster GPU Cluster Status Anonymised GPU machine cards showing how much of each GPU is in use Project Summary Your active projects and their status Resource Usage CPU / Memory / GPU trends (7-day or 30-day toggle) Activity Feed Recent actions by you and your team Active GPU Jobs Running workspaces with GPU, SM share, and memory

Figure 2: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, GPU cluster status, and active jobs.

docs.title: Step 5 — Check Your Project
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Projects in the left sidebar (Workspace section).
  2. A personal project is auto-created when your account is provisioned — look for a project named after your username.
  3. Click the project card to view its quota (GPU, CPU, Memory limits) and members.

Figure 3: Projects page showing personal project card with quota summary.

No project visible?

Ask your administrator to assign you to a project or group, or check that your account has been fully provisioned.

docs.title: Step 6 — Launch Your First Workspace
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Workspaces in the left sidebar.
  2. Click + New Workspace.
  3. Fill in the launch form:
Field What to Choose Project Select your project (personal or team) IDE Type JupyterLab or VS Code Image Base, PyTorch, TensorFlow, or custom CPU Number of CPU cores (e.g., 2) Memory RAM in GB (e.g., 8) GPU Number of GPUs and optional SM share (e.g., 1 GPU at 100% SM) Storage Mount your personal or group storage volume
  1. Click Create.
  2. Wait for the status badge to change from Starting (yellow) → Running (green).
  3. Click Open — your IDE opens in a new browser tab.

Figure 4: Workspace creation form with project, IDE type, and resource fields.

Workspace won't start?

  • Verify your project has sufficient quota remaining.
  • Check if the scheduling plan window is currently active (ask your admin).
  • If the image is custom, it may take longer to pull on first launch.

docs.title: Step 7 — Deploy a Container
docs.text:
A workspace gives you an interactive IDE. When you instead want to run your own container image — a long-running service or a batch job — deploy a container from a project config file. Config files can define Pod, Deployment, and Job workloads.

Requires Project Manager role

Creating and deploying config files needs the Manager role or higher. You already have this in your personal project; for a team project, ask a project manager.

  1. Go to Projects → [your project] → Config tab.
  2. Click + New Config. Paste a YAML manifest, or use the built-in Resource Wizard to fill in the fields without hand-writing YAML.

  3. Define your container:

    Field What to set Image A container image from the platform allowlist — see Requests to add a new one CPU / Memory Set both requests and limits; memory must be at least 128Mi (e.g. 512Mi) GPU (optional) Add a GPU request such as nvidia.com/rtx6000: "1", or map a reusable GPU claim Storage (optional) Use {{userVolume}} to mount your personal storage volume

  4. Click Save — each save creates a new, immutable version.

    Figure 5: The Config tab — creating a new config with the Resource Wizard.

  5. On the version row, click Deploy.

  6. In the deploy dialog, choose a scheduling queue. If your YAML uses GPU claim slots, map each slot to one of your reserved claims. Optionally click Dry-run first to validate without consuming quota.

  7. Click Deploy, then watch the instance until its pod reaches Running. Open logs or pod status from the instance view to check on it.

    Figure 6: The deploy dialog — choosing a scheduling queue and GPU claim.

Deploy rejected?

  • Every container must set both resources.requests.memory and resources.limits.memory (≥ 128Mi); missing values are rejected.
  • The image must be on the platform allowlist — submit an image request first if it is not.
  • Do not set metadata.namespace; the platform fills it in for you.
  • Deploying needs the Manager role and enough remaining project quota.

For config-file versioning, GPU requests, and reusable GPU claims in depth, see Projects → Config File Versioning.

docs.title: Step 8 — Manage Your Storage
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Storage in the left sidebar (Resources section).
  2. Click Start on your personal storage to launch the file browser.
  3. Click Browse — a FileBrowser UI opens where you can upload, download, rename, and organise files.
  4. Files stored here persist across workspace restarts.

Figure 7: FileBrowser interface showing personal storage contents.

docs.title: Step 9 — Join a Group (Optional)
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Groups in the left sidebar.
  2. Browse available groups or ask your admin to add you.
  3. Group members share a group storage volume — useful for datasets and shared models.
  4. Group managers can set per-user permissions (Read / Write / None) on shared storage.

docs.title: Service Quick Reference
docs.text:
Regular users only need the platform dashboard. Other service hostnames are reserved for the CLI, integrations, and administrators.

Service URL Purpose Dashboard https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw Main platform UI for users

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
VPN connects but dashboard DNS does not resolve

Ensure your VPN client accepts the DNS settings from the profile. Some clients require enabling DNS update scripts or importing the profile again. The user-facing entrypoint is https://dashboard.cscc.nthu.edu.tw.

CAPTCHA is wrong but I typed it correctly

CAPTCHA is case-insensitive. If the image is unclear, click it to get a new code. Avoid confusing 0/O or 1/I — the generator excludes ambiguous characters.

Login fails with 'Invalid credentials'

Verify you are using your username, not your email address. If your password was changed recently, the old one stops working immediately.

Workspace stuck in 'Starting' state

This usually means the container image is being pulled for the first time (can take several minutes for large GPU images). If it stays in Starting for more than 10 minutes, check with your admin that the scheduling queue is active and your project's plan window is open.

Session expired — redirected to login

Sessions expire after a while. Simply sign in again — your workspaces keep running in the meantime.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
Groups represent teams or departments. They provide shared storage access and can be added as members to multiple projects.

Access: All users can belong to groups. Group creation is typically done by admins; users can request a group via Requests.

docs.title: Group Membership Model
docs.text:
graph LR
    GroupAdmin["Group Admin\n(manages members\n& permissions)"]
    GroupMember["Group Member\n(access to group storage\n& projects)"]
    Group["Group"]

    GroupAdmin -->|manages| Group
    Group -->|includes| GroupMember
    Group -->|can be member of| Project["Projects"]
    Group -->|owns| GroupStorage["Group Storage PVCs"]

A group has three roles. Your group role also determines your default permissions on projects owned by that group.

Role Add / remove members Set storage permissions Access group storage Admin ✅ ✅ ✅ Manager ❌ ✅ ✅ User ❌ ❌ ✅

Teaching assistants usually need Admin

Setting students' storage permissions only needs Manager, but adding and removing members needs Admin. If you run a course, ask a platform admin for the Admin role.

docs.title: Groups List Page
docs.text:
Figure 1: Groups list showing group cards with member count, storage information, and policy badges.

Each group card shows: - Group name and description - Number of members - Associated storage volumes - Storage Policy and Registry Policy badges — set by an admin; they control which storage types are available for new group volumes and where the group's image builds are stored - Actions: View, Edit (admin only), Delete (admin only)

docs.title: View a Group
docs.text:
Click any group card to open its detail page. The detail page shows:

  1. Members tab — all group members with their roles
  2. Storage tab — volumes owned by this group and their permission settings

docs.title: Join a Group
docs.text:
Group membership is managed by group admins or platform admins. To join a group:

  1. Submit a request via Requests — select type Access Request.
  2. Describe which group you need access to and why.
  3. A group admin or platform admin will review and add you.

docs.title: Add Members to a Group
docs.text:
Requires Group Admin role.

  1. Open the group and click + Add Members (top-right of Members tab).
  2. Search for users by username or email.
  3. Select users from the results list.
  4. Click Add Members to confirm.

To add a whole class at once, use Paste users: paste the list into the text box (separated by newlines, commas, semicolons, or tabs) and click Resolve Users.

The results table lists only users who are not already members, so paging through the results never shows existing members or blank pages.

Figure 2: Add members dialog with user search and selection.

docs.title: Storage Permission Inheritance
docs.text:
Group storage permissions cascade to projects in a dual-path model:

flowchart TD
    GroupAdmin["Group Admin
sets permissions on group volume"] -->|batch operation| GroupPVC["Group volume
permissions (source of truth)"]
    GroupPVC -->|inherited, read-only rows| ProjectStoragePage["Project Storage page
(group member rows)"]
    ProjectAdmin["Project Admin
manages non-group members"] -->|direct management| DirectRows["Project volume permissions
(non-group members only)"]
    DirectRows --> ProjectStoragePage

Key rule: If you are a group member, your storage permissions on a project-bound volume always come from the group — they cannot be overridden at the project level. Project-level grants exist only for direct project members who are not in the owning group. Inherited rows appear read-only on the project storage page, with a badge linking to the group permissions page.

Permissions only apply to current group members: leaving the group removes your access immediately.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
I can see a group but can't add members.

Adding members requires the Group Admin role. Ask your current group admin or a platform admin to raise your role.

Why are my storage permissions greyed out on the project page?

You are a member of the group that owns this storage, so your permissions are managed at the group level. Open the group's Storage tab to see your effective permissions.

Can I belong to more than one group?

Yes. Group memberships are independent of one another, and there is no limit on how many you can join.

How do I leave a group?

Ask a group admin or platform admin to remove you — self-removal is not supported. You lose access to that group's storage immediately; anything in your personal storage is unaffected.

docs.title: Home Dashboard
docs.text:
The Home Dashboard is your starting point — it gives you a real-time snapshot of GPU availability, your resource usage, active jobs, and recent platform activity.

Access: All authenticated users.

docs.title: Dashboard Layout
docs.text:
graph TD
    subgraph TopRow["Top Row"]
        A["GPU Availability Card\n(cluster-wide GPU units)"]
        B["Project Summary\n(active projects count)"]
    end
    subgraph MiddleRow["Middle Row"]
        C["Resource Usage Chart\n(quota used vs. allocated)"]
        D["Activity Feed\n(recent platform events)"]
    end
    subgraph BottomRow["Bottom Row"]

    end

docs.title: Widget Reference
docs.text: Widget What It Shows Refresh GPU Availability Card Cluster-wide free vs. allocated GPU units, plus a preemptible-queue indicator On page load and every 10 seconds GPU Cluster Status Anonymised GPU machine cards showing how much of each GPU is in use On page load and every 10 seconds Project Summary Total projects you belong to On page load and every 10 seconds Resource Usage Chart GPU/CPU/memory quota consumed vs. total allocated per project, plus plan-window status On page load and every 10 seconds; countdown ticks every second Activity Feed Recent platform events — workspace starts, project changes, storage operations On page load and every 10 seconds My GPU Jobs Table of your currently running workspaces and batch jobs with GPU, SM share, and memory On page load and every 15 seconds

docs.title: Reading GPU Availability
docs.text:
The GPU Availability Card shows the current state of the cluster's GPU pool.

Figure 1: Home dashboard showing GPU availability, resource usage, and active jobs. Replace this placeholder with an actual screenshot.

Steps to read the GPU card:

  1. Look at the allocated / total fraction (e.g., 6 / 8 GPUs).
  2. Free GPUs = total − allocated. If free GPUs is 0, your workspace launch will be queued.
  3. The card also shows a Preemptible queues count. Even when every GPU is busy, a high-priority workload can still start by stopping a lower-priority one in a preemptible queue.
  4. Click the card to navigate to the Admin Monitoring page (admin users only) for per-node breakdown.

Effective GPU units

The card reports effective GPU units, not whole cards. A 1-GPU claim at 50% SM counts as 0.5 GPU, and only while a workload is actually attached to it.

docs.title: GPU Cluster Status
docs.text:
Beneath the availability card, the GPU Cluster Status grid shows anonymised GPU machines with:

  • A display label such as GPU node 1 and the GPU model
  • Each physical GPU card, with its index and model
  • How many shares of that machine's GPUs are taken, such as 3 / 8
  • A status bar and utilization percentage per GPU

Use this grid to spot which models are idle before submitting a workload, or to confirm a machine has room for a fractional claim. To protect privacy, the dashboard never shows other users' names or the names of their workloads.

docs.title: Resource Usage Chart
docs.text:
The chart displays your usage across all projects you belong to.

  • Each bar represents one project.
  • The bar fill shows consumed quota (GPU-hours, CPU-hours, or memory).
  • Each project row shows whether the bound resource plan is always active, closing, opening, or expired.
  • Plan-window countdowns update once per second without requiring a page refresh.

docs.title: Activity Feed
docs.text:
The activity feed shows the 20 most recent events relevant to you:

  • Workspace started / stopped / deleted
  • Project member added
  • Storage permission changed
  • Request status updated

Click any activity item to navigate directly to the related resource.

docs.title: My GPU Jobs
docs.text:
The My GPU Jobs table lists your active workspaces and batch jobs:

Column Description Name Job / workspace name Project Owning project GPU Effective GPU units consumed Status Running, Pending, Stopped, Error Started Start timestamp Actions Stop / Open links

Click Open next to a running workspace to open the IDE in a new tab.

Navigating from a job to its project

Click the project name in the Jobs table to jump to the Project Detail page where you can see quotas and config files.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
Why is my GPU count 0 on the availability card?

The card shows effective GPU availability. If every compatible GPU or SM share is already allocated, you will see 0 available. Check the Activity Feed — a workspace that finished recently may free capacity within a minute.

The activity feed is empty — is something wrong?

No. A fresh account with no project activity will show an empty feed. Create a project or launch a workspace and events will appear.

My running workspace is not in the jobs table.

The table refreshes every 15 seconds. Refresh the page (F5 or the browser refresh button) if the workspace still does not appear after the next poll.

docs.title: Projects
docs.text:
Projects are the primary unit of resource allocation on the platform. Every workspace you launch consumes quota from a project, and every config file or deployment belongs to a project.

Access: All authenticated users. A personal project is automatically created for you when you register.

docs.title: Project Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active : Create Project
    Active --> [*] : Admin Deletes

docs.title: Project Page Layout
docs.text:
Figure 1: Projects list showing grid view with GPU usage bars per project.

The Projects page supports two view modes:

  • Grid view — cards with project name, description, member count, GPU usage bar
  • List view — compact table with sortable columns

Toggle between views using the icons in the top-right of the toolbar.

docs.title: Create a Project
docs.text:
Creating a project requires the manage-projects permission. If you don't have it, the + New Project button is hidden (and the create page redirects back to your project list) — request a project from an admin instead. A personal project is created for you automatically when you register.

  1. Click Projects in the left sidebar.
  2. Click + New Project (top-right button; shown only with the manage-projects permission).
  3. Fill in the project form:
Field Description Name Short identifier (alphanumeric, hyphens allowed) Group Owning group (required) Description Optional — what this project is for
  1. Click Create. The project appears in your list immediately.

Quota is assigned by an admin

A new project starts with zero GPU quota. Contact your admin or submit a Request to have a Resource Plan bound to your project.

docs.title: Project Detail Tabs
docs.text:
Click a project card to open its detail page. The detail page includes core tabs for Overview, Config, Plan, Builds, GPU Claims, and Resources, plus role-dependent tabs such as Images, Members, and Storage.

Figure 2: Project detail page with Overview, Config, Plan, Builds, GPU Claims, Resources, and role-dependent tabs.

Tab Contents Overview Description, quota usage chart, current plan, member list summary Config Versioned config files describing what you want to run Plan Bound resource plan, schedule window, allowed GPU models, and quota envelope Builds Project-scoped image builds, archive or Dockerfile source selection, shared queue status, and live build logs GPU Claims Reusable GPU reservations you can prepare in advance and attach to a deployment later Resources Live per-member GPU/CPU/memory usage, expandable to what each member is running Images / Members / Storage Additional tabs shown when your role allows image management, membership management, quota controls, or storage access

Role thresholds: the Storage and Images tabs require Project Manager or above; the Members tab is visible to Project Admins only (platform admins must switch to Admin View via the avatar menu to be treated as an effective Project Admin). The frontend prevents an Admin from demoting themselves, so a project can never lose its last Admin.

docs.title: Build Project Images
docs.text: Use the Builds tab when a project needs a container image that is not already in the allowed image list. Project Managers and Project Admins can start builds when image builds are enabled for the project. Project Members can view build status and logs, but cannot start or delete builds.

docs.title: Source Options
docs.text: Source When to Use It Upload archive Upload a .tar.gz or .zip build context. Put the Dockerfile at the archive root. Dockerfile only Paste a Dockerfile directly. The platform creates a minimal build context.

docs.title: Build Settings
docs.text:
Field Notes Image Name Short repository name, for example trainer-api. The final registry path is generated by the platform. Tag Optional. Leave empty for the platform default, or set a release tag such as v1.0.1. Build source Upload archive or pasted Dockerfile.

Builds are submitted to a shared queue and run one at a time. Each build gets a fixed amount of CPU, memory, and scratch space that you cannot change from the form, and that capacity does not consume your project or personal quota.

Uploaded archives are checked for unsafe paths and size limits before the build starts.

The build history shows status, source type, destination image, and live logs. Failed builds show a short summary in the table — use the log button for the full output. If a build is retried, the log view keeps the previous attempt's failure reason before streaming the current one.

Builders and project managers can clear saved logs for completed or failed builds; build history and images are left untouched. The member who started a completed build, or a project manager, can also delete it from the history once nothing else references it.

Project Managers can submit project image allowlist requests and remove project image allowlist entries only for projects they currently manage. Project Members can view the project's image request history, but global catalog publications and other projects' image rules remain admin-controlled.

The Images tab splits into Available and Requests. Available lists the images this project may already pull. Requests lists every image request raised for the project -- pending ones first -- with its status, submission time and reviewer note; the tab label carries a badge with the pending count. Submitting a request through Add switches you to that tab so the new request is visible immediately.

A request you filed yourself can be taken back with Withdraw while it is still pending; you can submit it again afterwards. Requests filed by someone else, or already approved or rejected, offer no withdraw action.

Approved-as-global requests leave the project list

When an admin approves a request and ticks Make global, the request stops being project-scoped and disappears from this tab. The image itself then appears under Available.

Build access is project-governed

If the start form is hidden, the project either does not have Image Build Permission enabled or your project role cannot start builds. Build history and logs remain visible so you can still inspect previous jobs. Ask a project manager or platform admin to adjust the project setting or your role.

docs.title: GPU Claims
docs.text: The GPU Claims tab lists GPU reservations you can prepare for a project before deploying anything. A claim reserves GPU quota the moment you create it, but only starts counting GPU-hours once it is attached to a running Pod. You can pick a claim in the deploy dialog whenever a config file declares a GPU claim slot.

docs.title: Create a Claim
docs.text:
Field Notes Claim Name Name used when you attach this claim to a deployment. Letters, digits, and hyphens only. GPU Device Class The GPU model to reserve. The form defaults to a specific model; pick Any only when the model does not matter. GPU Count How many physical cards this claim reserves. A multi-GPU claim stays a single reservation. SM Share Compute slice from 1% to 100%. The resulting effective GPU count is shown beside the form. VRAM Mode Elastic shares GPU memory with other workloads; Hard cap enforces the percentage you pick. VRAM Share Used only with Hard cap. The reserved memory is derived from the smallest card of the selected model.

Every replica of a Deployment shares the same claim. A 2-GPU claim stays one 2-GPU reservation no matter how many replicas run, and quota and GPU-hours are counted once per claim rather than once per replica.

A claim that is not attached to anything uses 0 GPU-hours but still counts against project and per-user GPU quota. The table shows the owner, the node, the status (pending, bound, or terminating), how many workloads are using the claim, and a delete action. Unused claims can be deleted; a claim in use by a running Pod cannot.

Claim ownership

Project Members can create their own claims. Project Managers can also see and delete claims belonging to other members of the project.

docs.title: Plan Window Countdown
docs.text:
When a project's resource plan defines a schedule window, the Plan tab shows a live countdown to the next boundary:

  • Window closes in HH:MM:SS while the window is open.
  • Window opens in HH:MM:SS when the next window is upcoming.
  • Always active if no schedule restriction is defined.

The same countdown appears on the workspace launch form and on individual deployments. When the window closes, workloads in plan-bound queues are stopped; if the plan is removed or stops allowing your queue, anything still waiting to start is dropped too. A project with no active plan cannot start workloads at all.

Queues may also carry a runtime limit. When the queue you selected has one, your workload is stopped automatically after that many seconds. The limit is set by an admin and cannot be raised or disabled from your config file.

docs.title: Config File Versioning
docs.text:
Every save creates a new, immutable version. Old versions are never overwritten, so you can always look back at — or redeploy — an earlier one.

flowchart LR
    Edit["Edit or upload\na config file"] --> Save["Save"]
    Save --> Version["New immutable\nversion"]
    Version --> Deploy["Deploy any version"]

docs.title: Working with Config Files
docs.text:
1. Go to Projects → [your project] → Config tab.
  2. Click + New Config to upload a YAML file or paste content in the editor.
  3. Each save creates a new version — old versions are never overwritten.
  4. Click the History icon next to a config to view all versions.
  5. To deploy a specific version, click Deploy on the version row.
  6. In the deploy dialog, pick the scheduling queue. If the YAML contains GPU claim slots, choose one of your reserved GPU claims for each slot for this deploy only.

docs.title: Containers You Can Shell Into
docs.text:
To open a Terminal into a container, it has to stay running. A shell given no arguments — command: ["/bin/sh"] — exits immediately, so the container restarts over and over and every terminal attempt fails.

Either give the container real work:

command: ["sleep", "infinity"]

or keep the shell alive by enabling stdin and tty under Interactive shell in the Resource Wizard (stdin: true and tty: true in raw YAML). The wizard warns you when a bare shell would exit immediately.

Once the pod is running, open the project Resources tab and click Terminal on the Pod row. Deployment and Job rows have no terminal button — expand to the pod they created.

docs.title: Deploy Rules
docs.text:
Deploying, validating, inspecting, and deleting config-file instances needs the Project Manager role or higher. Quota is checked against everything you already have in flight, so a workload still waiting to start keeps holding its share until it finishes or is removed. Config files can deploy Pod, Deployment, and Job workloads; other kinds are not accepted.

Every container must set both a memory request and a memory limit of at least 128Mi; missing values are rejected during deploy and dry-run validation. Always include the unit — a bare memory: "1" means one byte and is rejected.

Leave platform-owned fields out of your YAML: do not set metadata.namespace, metadata.generateName, metadata.ownerReferences, or metadata.finalizers. For storage, use {{userVolume}} to mount your personal volume; naming a volume directly works only in group-owned projects, and only for volumes the owning group already has.

docs.title: Inline GPU Requests vs. Reusable GPU Claims
docs.text:
There are two ways a config file can ask for a GPU.

  • Inline GPU requests are written straight into the container's resource requests, for example nvidia.com/rtx6000: "1". The platform counts them toward quota, checks the model against your plan's allowed models, and sets up the GPU when you deploy.
  • Reusable GPU claims come from the GPU Claims tab. In the Resource Wizard, choose Pick at deploy and give the slot a name such as train-a; in raw YAML, annotate the Pod or the Deployment's pod template with platform-go/dra-claim-name: '{{ gpuClaimName "train-a" }}'. The slot name is only a label — you map it to one of your own claims in the deploy dialog.

A few things worth knowing:

  • {{gpuClaimName}} with no name still works as the default slot. Two workloads can share a slot deliberately, or use different slots to get different claims.
  • Every replica of a Deployment shares one claim. If only some replicas should use a claim, split them into separate Deployments.
  • Configs that request no GPU need no allowed-model list, and never receive a GPU claim.

Config files and deployments require Project Manager role

Only project members with Manager or higher role can create, edit, deploy, validate, inspect, or delete config-file instances.

docs.title: Managing Members
docs.text:
1. Open the project and go to the Members tab.
  2. Click + Add Members (requires Project Admin role).
  3. Search for users by username or email.
  4. Select a role for each user:
Role What they can do User Launch workspaces, view configs Manager Edit configs, manage deployments Admin Add/remove members, set member quotas, delete project
  1. Click Confirm to save.

Project Admins can select several rows at once to remove members, change roles, or set per-user quotas in bulk. Managers and Admins can see everyone's quota; a Project User sees only their own. A quota of 0 means that resource is unlimited for that member, still capped by the project plan.

Group-inherited members. Members who joined through the owning group can be included in a bulk quota change, but not in bulk remove or role changes — their membership and role are managed in the group instead.

Removing a direct member also removes their workspace area in the project, any project storage permission overrides, and their per-user quota. Group-inherited members must be removed from the owning group instead.

docs.title: Group Inheritance and Effective Project Role
docs.text:
When a project is owned by a group, the platform resolves each caller's effective project role as follows:

  1. If the user has an explicit project member record, that role wins (admin / manager / user).
  2. Otherwise, for personal projects, the personal owner is treated as admin.
  3. Otherwise, the user's group role in the owning group is used as the effective project role. A Group Admin therefore acts as a Project Admin on every project owned by that group, even without an explicit project_members row.

This is why a Group Admin can set per-user quotas on a project owned by their group, and see the batch selection controls in the Members tab, without being added as a direct member.

Offboarding tip: when someone leaves the lab, ask an admin to remove them from the owning group — access to every project joined through that group disappears automatically, with no per-project cleanup.

docs.title: Deleting a Project
docs.text:
Only a Project Admin can delete a project: stop all of its workspaces first, then Project Overview → Edit → Delete and type the project name to confirm. Effects:

  • Config version history and deployment records are permanently removed.
  • PVCs are not deleted (they remain on the Storage page).
  • A group-owned project may require a platform admin to revoke the group binding before deletion is allowed.

docs.title: Resources Tab
docs.text:
The Resources tab summarizes live usage by project member:

Column Meaning User Project member GPU Effective GPU units currently used CPU Requested or observed CPU cores Memory Memory in MiB Pods Number of active pods that member is running

Project Admins, Project Managers, and platform Admin/Manager roles see every project member; regular Project Users see only their own row. Expand a row to inspect what is running, or terminate the resources you are allowed to manage. Terminating a workload here releases the quota it was holding.

For Pod rows, hover, focus, or tap the status badge to see recent events. This is useful when a Pod looks like it is still starting but is really failing to pull its image.

docs.title: GPU Quota Overview
docs.text:
The Overview tab shows a quota bar for each resource type:

Resource What It Tracks GPU Effective GPU units consumed vs. plan limit CPU CPU cores consumed by running workspaces Memory RAM consumed by running workspaces

If the GPU bar is full (100%), new workspace launches will queue and wait for resources to free up.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
I don't see a + New Project button.

The button is shown only to users with the manage-projects permission. If you don't have it, ask an admin to create a project for you — your personal project is created automatically when you register.

How do I view old config file versions?

On the Config tab, click the clock icon (History) next to any config file to see all past versions with their timestamps.

My project quota is 0 GPUs. How do I get more?

Submit a Resource Request via Requests. An admin will review and bind a Resource Plan to your project.

What's the difference between a workspace's GPU and a GPU Claim?

A workspace reserves its GPU only for as long as the workspace exists. A GPU Claim is a standalone reservation that survives across deployments — useful when several jobs need the same fractional GPU and you want to avoid rescheduling churn.

Why is the Deploy button disabled?

Either the project has no active plan bound, or the plan window is currently closed and only the default queue is selectable. Check the Plan tab for the next opening time.

docs.title: Requests
docs.text:
The Requests feature lets you submit structured requests to platform administrators — for more GPU quota, new storage, image access, feature suggestions, or bug reports.

Access: All authenticated users.

docs.title: Request Types
docs.text: Type When to Use Resource Need more GPU/CPU quota, additional storage capacity, or new resource allocation Access Need to join a group, access a shared PVC, or get elevated permissions Feature Suggest a new platform feature Bug Report a platform issue Question Ask a general question to platform administrators Other Anything that doesn't fit the above categories

docs.title: Request Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Pending : You submit the form
    Pending --> Processing : Admin picks it up
    Pending --> Completed : Admin resolves it
    Pending --> Rejected : Admin rejects it
    Processing --> Completed : Admin resolves it
    Processing --> Rejected : Admin rejects it
    Processing --> Pending : Admin puts it back
    Rejected --> Pending : Admin reopens it
    Completed --> [*]

Completed is final: a resolved request cannot be reopened, and its message thread is closed. A rejected request can still be reopened by an admin.

docs.title: My Requests Page
docs.text:
Figure 1: Requests list showing request cards with type tags, status badges, and creation dates.

The Requests page lists all requests you have submitted, with:

  • Type tag — coloured label (Resource, Access, Feature, Bug, Question, Other)
  • Status badge — Pending, Processing, Completed, Rejected
  • Title — your request title
  • Created — submission date
  • Click any request to open the detail view with the message thread

docs.title: Submit a New Request
docs.text:
1. Click Requests in the left sidebar.
  2. Click + New Request (top-right).

Figure 2: New request creation form with type selector, title, and description fields.

  1. Fill in the form:
Field Description Project Optional — link the request to a project you belong to so admins see its current GPU quota. The selected project's GPU bar appears beside the picker. Type Select the request category from the tag grid (Resource, Access, Feature, Bug, Question, Other). Title Short, descriptive title (e.g., "Request 4 GPU units for project LLM-Training"). Description Rich-text editor — supports formatting, code blocks, and inline image uploads. Drag screenshots in to attach evidence. Inline uploads accept JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP image content up to 10 MiB.
  1. Click Submit.

Be specific in your description

A clear description speeds up admin review. For resource requests, include: which project needs the quota, how many GPUs you need, for how long, and the research objective.

docs.title: Image Requests
docs.text:
When you need a base image that is not in the platform's allowed list, use the Request Image form (linked from the project Images tab and the dashboard image catalog). It is a structured request type that an admin can act on without back-and-forth.

Field Description Registry Optional. Defaults to docker.io when blank. Repository Image path without the tag, e.g. pytorch/pytorch, or nvidia/* to request a whole family. Tag Optional. Defaults to latest, or * when the repository is a wildcard.

A live preview shows the canonical image reference admins will review. Once approved, the image is added to the platform allowlist and becomes selectable from the workspace and deploy forms.

docs.title: Track Your Request
docs.text:
1. Open your request from the list.
  2. The detail page shows the full message thread.
  3. If an admin asks for more information, you'll see their message in the thread — reply using the text box at the bottom. The thread closes once the request is resolved.

Figure 3: Request detail page showing the message thread between user and admin.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
How long does it take for a request to be reviewed?

Review times vary with admin workload. Most requests are handled within 1–2 business days; if you have had no reply after three days, follow up in the message thread.

Can I edit or cancel a request after submitting it?

No. Use the message thread to add or correct details instead. Once a request is Completed the thread closes, so you would need to open a new request.

My request was rejected. Can I resubmit?

Yes. Read the admin's reason, adjust your request accordingly, and submit a new one. Referencing the previous request number helps.

I don't see a notification when my request is resolved.

Check your notification settings under Settings → Notifications and make sure request updates are enabled.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The Settings page lets you manage your profile, change your password, configure notifications, and set your language preference.

Access: All authenticated users. Navigate via Settings in the left sidebar (Infrastructure section).

docs.title: Settings Tabs
docs.text:
Figure 1: Settings page showing the tabs: Profile, Security, Notifications, and Preferences.

Tab Purpose Profile Update display name and view account information Security Change your password; manage API tokens and CLI access Notifications Enable or disable email and in-app notification types Preferences Select your display language

docs.title: Profile
docs.text:
The Profile tab shows:

  • Display Name — editable; shown in the UI wherever your name appears
  • Username — read-only; your login identifier
  • Email — contact address; may be read-only if your account is managed via SSO

To update your display name:

  1. Click the Profile tab.
  2. Edit the Display Name field.
  3. Click Save Changes.

docs.title: Change Password
docs.text:
1. Click the Security tab.
  2. Enter your Current Password.
  3. Enter your New Password (minimum 8 characters, mix of letters and numbers recommended).
  4. Repeat the new password in Confirm Password.
  5. Click Update Password.

Password requirements

A password change here applies everywhere you sign in, including the VPN. Accounts managed by an external identity provider cannot change their password here.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
The Notifications tab lets you control which events trigger notifications.

Notification Type Description Request Updates When an admin changes the status of your submitted request Workspace Events When a workspace starts, stops, or encounters an error Project Changes When you are added to or removed from a project Storage Changes When storage permissions affecting you are modified

Toggle each type on or off. Changes save immediately.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
Select your preferred display language from the dropdown. The UI will reload in the selected language.

Available languages depend on your platform configuration. Contact your admin if your language is missing.

docs.title: API Tokens & CLI (under the Security tab)
docs.text: The Security tab is the entry point for the cscc-cli tool. It helps you manage CLI credentials and copy setup commands.

docs.title: Active API Tokens
docs.text:
The token list shows every active API token issued for your account, with prefix, last-used time, and expiry. From here you can:

  • Create token — generate a new token with an optional name. The full token value is shown once; copy it before closing the dialog.
  • CLI import — the reveal dialog includes a copyable cscc-cli login --api-url ... --token cscc_... command after the token is created.
  • Revoke — invalidate any token. CLI sessions using that token will stop working on their next call.

Tokens default to a 90-day lifetime, and your account is capped at 20 active tokens at a time.

One-time reveal

The token value is shown once and is never stored in a readable form. If you lose it, revoke the token and create a new one.

Official cscc-cli releases already trust the platform's certificate, so normal CLI setup needs no extra download from this page. The setup commands shown here already point at the correct API address for this deployment.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
I can't change my password — the field is greyed out.

Your account is managed by an external identity provider, so its password is changed there rather than here.

I forgot my password.

The sign-in page has no self-service reset. Ask a platform admin to reset it for you; the new password then applies everywhere you sign in, including the VPN.

The email shown on the Settings page is wrong.

If your email comes from the account directory you cannot edit it here — ask an admin to update it.

I'm not receiving email notifications even though they're enabled.

Check your spam folder first. If nothing arrives, contact your admin — email delivery may not be configured.

Can I delete my account?

Only an admin can delete an account. Submit a request describing what you need; the admin handles data retention before removing it.

I lost my API token. Can I recover it?

No. Token values are shown only once. Revoke the lost token under the Security tab and create a new one.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
The platform provides two types of persistent storage volumes. Anything you write inside a mounted volume persists independently of workspaces — it survives the workspace being stopped or deleted.

A workspace with no storage attached keeps nothing

Personal storage mounts at /home/<your username>; each group volume mounts at /mnt/shared/<volume name>. Anything written elsewhere is lost as soon as the workspace stops, restarts, or is deleted. If you have no volume mounted at all, nothing you save will survive — the platform warns you before starting such a workspace.

Access: Personal storage is provisioned by an admin, so not every account has one — check the Storage → Personal tab and ask an admin to set one up if it is missing. Group storage access is managed by group admins, and only current members of a group can hold permissions on its volumes.

docs.title: Storage Types
docs.text: Personal Storage Group Storage Owner Your user account A group Provisioned by Admin (batch init) Admin (on request) Access You only Group members (permissions vary) Best for Personal datasets, notebooks, experiments Shared datasets, team collaboration Managed from Storage → Personal tab Storage → Group tab

docs.title: Storage List Page
docs.text:
Figure 1: Storage page with Personal and Group tabs. Each PVC shows capacity, status, and a Browse button.

The Storage page has two tabs:

  • Personal — your private PVCs
  • Group — PVCs belonging to groups you are a member of

Each PVC row shows: - Name and description - Capacity (e.g., 50Gi) - Status: Available, Bound, Pending - Browse button — open the file browser for this PVC - Permissions button (group storage, for admins)

docs.title: Storage Lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    Request["Request storage\nvia the Requests form"] -->|Admin approves| Provisioned["Volume created"]
    Provisioned -->|Bound to a project| Available["Selectable when\nlaunching a workspace"]
    Available -->|Workspace mounts it| InUse["Data persists\nacross restarts"]
    InUse -->|Admin deletes it| Released["Volume removed\n(data lost)"]

PVC deletion is permanent

When an admin deletes a PVC, all data inside it is permanently destroyed. Always back up important data before requesting PVC removal.

docs.title: Browsing Storage Files
docs.text:
Click Browse next to any PVC to open the file browser.

Figure 2: Storage file browser showing directory listing with upload, download, and delete capabilities.

Opening the file browser is blocked when your permission on that volume is None.

The file browser supports: - Navigate directories - Upload files (drag and drop or file picker) - Download files and folders - Create new directories - Delete files (use caution — deletions are immediate)

docs.title: Using Storage in Workspaces
docs.text:
When launching a new workspace, you can mount one or more PVCs:

  1. In the New Workspace form, find the Storage section.
  2. Click + Add Storage.
  3. Select the PVC from the dropdown.
  4. Set the Mount Path (e.g., /data or /workspace/datasets).
  5. Repeat for additional PVCs.

Mount path convention

Use consistent mount paths across workspaces so your code always finds data at the same location regardless of which workspace is running.

docs.title: Storage Profiles and Lanes
docs.text:
Group storage is provisioned by platform admins — the Create Storage button needs the storage.manage permission, which a group admin role does not grant. Request a new volume through Requests. When provisioning, the admin picks a Storage Profile that maps to a backing storage class and a lane. Each lane is tuned for a different workload shape.

Profile Backend Lane Best for CephFS RWX Shared cluster filesystem shared-rwx Home directories, datasets, and checkpoints that many workloads need to see at once — the only lane that can be shared across projects Node-local Scratch Disk on the machine running the job local-scratch Fast per-job /scratch — ephemeral: lost if the machine goes away or the volume is deleted Longhorn (Fast RWO) Fast block storage fast-rwo Scratch that must survive a restart of the workload Default Cluster default varies Let the platform pick

The profile picker shows availability and a recommendation per option; unavailable profiles are greyed out with the reason.

docs.title: Training Storage Pattern
docs.text:
For model training on gpu1, gpu2, and gpu3, admins can provision group storage on cephfs. This is the preferred shared path for datasets, checkpoints, and final artifacts that need to be visible across nodes.

For checkpoint-heavy jobs, use this layout:

Path Storage Purpose /datasets CephFS group RWX Shared read-mostly training data /checkpoints CephFS group RWX Durable checkpoints and resumable state /scratch Node-local scratch (local-scratch) Temporary hot files during a single job — fast, but ephemeral

Copy only the final results from scratch back to the shared CephFS mount. Repeated reads stay fast locally, and the shared filesystem is not hammered with writes.

docs.title: Fast-Stage Cache
docs.text:
Fast-stage copies data from a shared group volume into a project-local Fast RWO volume, so a single training job reads at local speed instead of over the shared filesystem.

  1. On the project's Storage tab, click Data Path next to a bound RWX volume.
  2. Select Fast-stage Cache in the modal.
  3. Fill in the form:
Field Notes Target Namespace Whose space the fast volume is created in — pick yourself unless you are staging for a teammate. Fast PVC Name Defaults to fast-<source volume>. Letters, digits, and hyphens only. Fast Capacity (Gi) Must be at least as large as the source volume. Checksum Mode Size + mtime is the default; choose SHA-256 for strict verification or None to skip checks.
  1. Click Start Fast Stage. The platform runs a one-off copy Job and reports its status. The transfer needs an active project plan and a small amount of free CPU and memory quota.

Sync results back

Fast-stage is a read cache. When training finishes, copy final artifacts back to the shared RWX mount — the fast volume is project-local and your teammates cannot see it.

docs.title: Storage Permissions
docs.text:
Group storage volumes have per-user permission levels:

Permission Description Read Can mount and read files; cannot write Write Can mount, read, and write files Admin Full control including permission management

When a group admin explicitly sets your permission on a volume to None, that denial wins over anything the project or group would otherwise grant. Clearing it restores your normal permission.

To view or request permission changes, contact your group admin. Group admins can update permissions in bulk from the group's Storage tab (see Groups).

docs.title: Request Additional Storage
docs.text:
If you need more storage capacity or a new group storage PVC:

  1. Go to Requests → + New Request.
  2. Select type Resource Request.
  3. Describe the storage you need (size, purpose, group name).
  4. Submit — an admin will review and provision the PVC.

docs.title: Common Questions
docs.text:
My storage shows as Pending. When will it be available?

Pending means the volume is still being created. This usually takes under a minute. If it stays Pending for more than 5 minutes, contact your admin.

My storage is full but I can't find any large files.

Open a workspace terminal and run du -sh /home/<your username>/*. Hidden folders such as .cache and .local, or large notebook checkpoints, are the usual culprits.

I can see a group volume but can't browse it.

You need at least Read permission on that volume. Contact your group admin to check your permissions.

Is my data still there after I delete a workspace?

Yes. Storage volumes exist independently of workspaces — data is lost only when the volume itself is deleted.

Can I mount the same volume in several workspaces at once?

Yes, provided the volume supports multiple mounts (RWX). Check the Access mode column on the Storage page.

Files I uploaded via the browser aren't appearing in my workspace.

Check that your workspace has the volume mounted at the path you expect. Volumes are attached when the workspace starts, but files uploaded afterwards appear immediately — no restart needed.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
Workspaces (also called IDEs) are interactive cloud development environments — JupyterLab, VSCode, or custom-image environments — backed by GPU resources.

Access: All project members with sufficient project quota.
